# Presentation Abstracts Skill

This skill provides guidance for crafting effective conference presentation abstracts that grab attention and communicate value clearly.

## When to Use This Skill

-   Writing a new presentation abstract from scratch
-   Refining an existing abstract for resubmission
-   Reviewing an abstract before submission
-   Helping structure the core message of a talk

## Before You Start: Conference Research (Optional)

Before diving into abstract writing, **ask the user:**

> "Are you targeting a specific conference? If so, I can research past talks and abstracts to help tailor your submission. Would you like me to do that first?"

If yes, use the **conference-research** skill to:

1. Analyze what talks have been accepted in past years
2. Understand the conference's typical topics, levels, and abstract styles
3. Identify how to position the talk for the best chance of acceptance

Then return here with those insights to inform the abstract writing.

## Key Files

-   [kent-beck-guidance.md](kent-beck-guidance.md) — Kent Beck's advice on writing compelling paper/presentation abstracts

## The Four-Sentence Abstract Structure

Based on Kent Beck's approach, aim for an abstract with four key sentences (flexibly applied):

1. **State the problem** — What challenge or gap exists?
2. **Why it matters** — Why should the audience care about this problem?
3. **Your startling sentence** — The core insight, solution, or claim (this is the hook!)
4. **The implication** — What does this mean for the audience? What will they gain?

### Example Structure

> [Problem]: Many developers struggle with testing code that uses HttpClient.
> [Why it matters]: Without proper testing, bugs slip through and refactoring becomes risky.
> [Startling sentence]: You can fully mock HttpClient in three simple patterns without any external libraries.
> [Implication]: Attendees will leave with reusable patterns they can apply immediately in their own projects.

## Writing Guidelines

### Know Your Audience

-   **Primary audience:** The program committee / selection reviewers
-   They're experts who've seen hundreds of submissions
-   You have ~30 seconds to grab their interest
-   They sort into "A pile" (excited to read) and "B pile" (chore to read)

### Find Your One Startling Sentence

-   Boil your entire talk down to ONE compelling statement
-   It should make the reader's eyes open wide
-   Be specific and concrete — vague claims are forgettable
-   Don't be afraid to make a bold, falsifiable claim

### Keep It Short and Clear

-   Short abstracts get into the "A pile"
-   Resist the temptation to argue for your conclusion in the abstract
-   Let the abstract create intrigue — make them want to hear the full talk
-   Don't try to cram everything about your topic into the abstract

### The Full Talk Structure (for context)

When the abstract needs to hint at depth, remember the full talk should follow:

1. **Problem** — Make the audience understand and believe it's important
2. **Solution** — Your approach to solving it
3. **Defense** — Evidence that it actually works
4. **Related work** — What makes your approach novel

## Abstract Checklist

-   [ ] Follows the four-sentence structure (or close to it)
-   [ ] Has one clear, startling sentence/claim
-   [ ] Written for experts who need to be intrigued quickly
-   [ ] Short and scannable (not a wall of text)
-   [ ] Makes the reader want to know "how can they say that?"
-   [ ] Clear benefit/takeaway for attendees
-   [ ] Avoids jargon that only you understand
-   [ ] Problem is relatable and important

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

-   **"The Foo System In All Its Glory"** — Trying to include everything instead of focusing on one hook
-   **Vague claims** — "This talk will be interesting" vs. specific value
-   **Arguing in the abstract** — Save the proof for the talk itself
-   **Writing to the general audience first** — Get past the committee first!
-   **Playing it safe** — Boring, hedged statements don't grab attention

## Refinement Process

When refining an existing abstract:

1. Identify the startling sentence — if you can't find one, that's the problem
2. Check the four-sentence structure — is anything missing?
3. Cut ruthlessly — every word should earn its place
4. Read it as a tired reviewer — does it make you want to learn more?
